title: Solar Photovoltaic Based Modular Electric Vehicle Battery Charging Using Interleaved Boost and Phase‐Shifted Full‐Bridge Converters
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper proposes direct charging of lithium‐ion batteries in electric vehicles (EVs) using standalone solar photovoltaic (PV) systems at distributed charging stations. A PV plant can be operated in an adaptive optimal mode to dynamically regulate its output power to match the aggregate charging power drawn by multiple lithium‐ion batteries, as reflected in the DC‐link voltage. To stabilize the DC‐link voltage and balance power between PV generation and battery load, a master–slave control strategy is used. In this setup, the DC‐link voltage controller acts as the master, generating a corrective duty cycle to reduce voltage changes. The MPPT (Maximum Power Point Tracking) controller, acting as the slave, provides the base duty cycle to extract the maximum power possible from the PV array. The resulting composite duty ratio drives a multiple‐phase interleaved boost DC–DC converter, improving power conversion efficiency and reducing input current ripple. A distributed phase‐shifted full‐bridge converter (PSFBC) is used to charge the batteries following the constant current–constant voltage (CC–CV) method. The proposed architecture is implemented using a modular three‐leg inverter, which is scalable and allows integration of higher‐rated PV arrays and additional battery charging channels without requiring any major modification in the control strategy, owing to the flexibility of the master–slave coordination mechanism. A multiple‐modular boost‐PSFB converter using four three‐phase inverter modules has been used for implementing the four‐phase IBC‐PSFB converter for 10.44 kW solar PV to charge four 72 V, 100 Ah Li‐ion batteries through MATLAB Simulink software. The control algorithm is also validated in real‐time using Typhoon‐HIL in virtual HIL mode for implementing a two‐phase IBC‐PSFB converter, based on a practical setup comprising a 2.2 kW solar PV system and two 72 V, 26 Ah Li‐ion batteries.
title_zh: Solar Photovoltaic Based Modular Electric Vehicle Battery Charging Using Interleaved Boost and Phase‐Shifted Full‐Bridge Converters

title: Assessing Photovoltaic Power Plants With Battery Energy Storage for Capacity Reserve Auctions in Brazil
abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid expansion of variable renewable energy in Brazil has induced severe intraday curtailment, characterized by a pronounced “Duck Curve” driven by transmission limits and regional centralization of generation. This study evaluates the techno‐economic and regulatory feasibility of utility‐scale photovoltaic (PV) plants integrated with battery energy storage systems (BESS) to mitigate curtailment and meet the firm capacity requirements of the Brazilian Capacity Reserve Auctions. Four 30 MW AC (alternating current) hybrid plants, each coupled with a 150 MWh BESS, were simulated across Brazil's four electrical submarkets using the System Advisor Model (SAM) and a customized financial model. Results demonstrate that this configuration guarantees a 4‐h daily evening dispatch with a loss of load probability (LoLP) below 0.5%. Furthermore, the system operates at a strict maximum discharging C‐rate of 0.20 C, perfectly aligning with manufacturer guidelines to preserve battery lifespan and control depth of discharge (DoD) degradation. Economically, relying exclusively on spot market arbitrage is unviable, as the levelized cost of storage (LCOS) exceeds regulatory price ceilings. However, backed by fixed auction revenues and subsidized financing, the projects achieve highly profitable internal rates of return (IRR) between 23.53% and 24.29% across all regions. Supported by the recent enactment of Law No. 15.269/2025, which formally establishes energy storage as an autonomous sector activity, these findings confirm that BESS deployment under capacity reserve auctions is an immediately viable solution to ensure grid reliability and unlock further renewable expansion.

title: Physics-constrained long-horizon state of health prediction with explicit recovery correction for lithium-ion batteries
abstract: Reliable long-horizon state of health (SOH) prognosis of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) is important for battery management and retire assessment. Reversible capacity recovery can distort recursive SOH trajectories, causing systematic drift errors and biased end-of-life (EOL) timing. To address this issue, we propose a physics-constrained SOH prediction framework that jointly models battery aging evolution and recovery-induced deviations. Firstly, multi-time-scale probe integration (MTPI) is employed to extract three physical features of LIBs directly from charging-pulse relaxation data without signal decomposition. Then, a BiLSTM with an irreversibility-guided loss suppresses recursive predictions through a soft irreversibility prior. Finally, a KWW–Arrhenius-constrained recovery network (KARN) localizes recovery events, estimates their amplitudes, and calibrates the LIB trajectory. The Tsinghua Berkeley Shenzhen Institute (TBSI) dataset contains 32 NCM811 cells tested at 25–55 °C and is divided into cell-disjoint training, validation, and test sets. External validation uses the SNU NMC811/Gr–SiOₓ, UConn LFP/graphite, and CALCE LiCoO₂/graphite datasets. The proposed framework achieves a chain RMSE of 0.97% SOH, an end-point error of 0.89%, and a MAPE of 0.91%. These values correspond to the reductions of 84.1%, 91.4%, and 85.1%, respectively, relative to the degradation-only baseline. Ablation and sensitivity analyses show that recovery detection and drift compensation make the main contributions to the accuracy improvements, whereas KWW–Arrhenius regularization mainly improves the physical plausibility of the learned recovery kinetics. All three representative held-out cells crossed the 80% SOH EOL threshold within the observed test horizon. The proposed framework also reduces the average capacity error from 80.4 mAh to 6.9 mAh. MTPI achieved R 2 = 0.992 on SNU and R 2 = 0.911 on UConn, while a protocol-adapted KARN variant achieved a recovery RMSE of 9.34 mAh on CALCE. These findings support long-horizon health assessment near the retirement stage.

title: Feature driven machine learning framework for accurate and computationally efficient remaining useful life prediction of lithium-ion batteries
abstract: Accurate estimation of the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) of lithium-ion batteries is essential for improving the reliability, safety, and cost-effectiveness of electric vehicles (EVs). Although several machine learning models have been reported for RUL prediction, many require extensive feature engineering or high computational effort, which limits their practical use in battery management systems. This work presents a predictive machine learning framework that balances prediction accuracy with computational efficiency. The proposed framework uses sensor-derived features from the NASA battery degradation dataset. The data are first preprocessed through exploratory data analysis and normalization to improve their quality. Feature analysis identifies the maximum discharge voltage and the minimum charge voltage as the two most influential indicators of battery degradation. These features are then used to train three regression models, namely k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN), Support Vector Regression (SVR), and Random Forest (RF). The models are evaluated using multiple statistical performance metrics. Among them, the RF model delivers the best overall performance with a coefficient of determination ( \(R^{2}\) ) of 0.9421 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 77.47. The kNN model achieves comparable prediction accuracy while requiring less training time. However, the SVR model exhibits lower prediction accuracy incurring higher computational cost. The proposed framework is further validated using independent battery datasets, where the predicted RUL closely follows the observed degradation trend. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach provides accurate, reliable, and computationally efficient RUL estimation, making it suitable for real-time battery health monitoring and predictive battery management in electric vehicles. In the future, this framework has the potential to contribute to effective and scalable battery health management systems. Furthermore, it could be extended to deep learning and adaptive models to be used under diverse operating conditions.
title_zh: Feature driven machine learning framework for accurate and computationally efficient remaining useful life prediction of lithium-ion batteries
